title: My day
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Russian has ONE present tense where English has two. Я работаю covers both "I work" (every day) and "I am working" (right now), and there is no second shape to reach for. Everything on this rung is a habit, and the same forms would do for what is happening this minute.

Verbs come in two ending patterns and the pattern is a property of the verb, learned with it — there is no way to tell from the meaning. Pattern I: работаю · работаете · работает, читаю · читаете · читает. Pattern II: говорю · говорите · говорит. The difference shows in the you-form and the he/she-form: -ете for one pattern, -ите for the other.

Some verbs write ё in their endings — пью · пьёте, встаю · встаёте — and this course always writes the two dots. Most Russian printing leaves them off and expects you to know; here they stay on, because ё and е are different letters and dropping the dots would make one word look like another.

The times of day are single words: утром (in the morning), днём (in the afternoon), вечером (in the evening), ночью (at night). They are frozen shapes of утро, день, вечер and ночь — the leftovers of a case this level does not teach — so learn them as they are and do not try to build them. They usually open the sentence.

Clock time is в plus the hour, and the word for "hour" changes with the number in front of it: один час, два часа, семь часов. That is your first sight of a rule M8 will spell out — after 1 the noun is in its plain shape, after 2–4 it takes one ending, after 5 and up another. Here, just learn часов with the bigger numbers.

This level always writes the subject pronoun. Russian can drop я, because the ending already names the person, and in speech it often does — but the drop is a stylistic judgement rather than a rule, and M5's past tense will not name the person at all. Keep the pronoun until you can hear when to lose it.

words.note: "I get up", from вставать. One Russian word for what English needs two for — there is no separate "up". The you-form and the he/she-form write ё: встаёте, встаёт, and this course always prints the dots.
Early. It describes the verb rather than a noun, so it never changes shape — a whole class of Russian words that ask nothing of you.

sentences.trap: English "get up" is a verb plus a little word, and hunting for the Russian "up" is wasted effort. встаю is the whole thing.
sentences.sound: ya fsta-YOO RA-na. The в at the start is said as an f, because the с after it is voiceless — Russian consonants take their colour from their neighbours.

variations.changed: swap the time word — the verb does not move
встаю → встаёте for the polite you, and the ё appears in the ending
the he/she ending — встаёт, with the same ё

mistake.why: вверх is a real word for "upwards", and it has no business here. встаю already means "get up".

sentences.usage: Describing your routine — the first line of any "my day" conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: One Russian word swallows the English verb and its little word whole.

sentences.cue: I get up at seven o'clock

words.note: One tiny preposition with two jobs in this course. Here it points at a clock time — в семь часов, "at seven". In M7 it points at a place — в магазине, "in the shop" — and it bends the word after it there, the way из does. Same word, two seats; the shape of what follows tells you which.
Seven. The ь on the end is not a sound of its own — it softens the м. Numbers from five upward all end this way.

"Hour", and the number in front decides its shape: один час, два часа, семь часов. English says "seven o'clock" with the noun untouched; Russian makes the noun answer to the number, and M8 turns that into a rule for every noun.

sentences.trap: The noun changes because of the number, which English never does. "Seven o'clock" and "one o'clock" use the same word; семь часов and один час do not.
sentences.sound: ya fsta-YOO f syem chee-SOF. The в is said as an f here too, and the final в of часов is an f as well — Russian ends words voiceless.

variations.cue: I get up at six o'clock
variations.changed: swap the number — часов stays, because six is also above four

variations.cue: I get up at two o'clock
variations.changed: два takes the other ending: часа, not часов

variations.cue: Do you get up at seven?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, asked rather than told

mistake.why: час is the shape that goes after один. After семь it is часов.

sentences.usage: Any time of day — the frame every appointment and every routine runs on.
sentences.mnemonic: The number is in charge. The noun does what it is told.

sentences.cue: In the morning I drink tea

words.note: "In the morning", in one word: there is no preposition and no article anywhere in it. It is a frozen shape of утро, left over from a case this course does not teach, so learn it whole. It normally opens the sentence.

"I drink", from пить. The ь inside пью and пьёте is a separator: it keeps the п and the vowel apart, so the word is said "pyoo" and not "pu". The you-form and the he/she-form carry ё, and this course writes the dots.

sentences.trap: "In the morning" is three English words and one Russian one, with nothing standing in for "in" or "the". Building it out of в plus утро is the English reflex and it is wrong.
sentences.sound: OO-tram ya pyoo chai. The unstressed о of утром flattens to "a", and пью is one syllable, not two.

variations.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
variations.changed: swap the drink — neither word around it moves

variations.cue: In the evening I drink tea
variations.changed: swap the time of day — the frame is the same for all four

variations.cue: Do you drink tea in the morning?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, and the time word moved to the end — both orders are ordinary

mistake.why: There is no preposition in this phrase. "In the morning" is утром, one word, and building it out of в plus утро is the English habit.

sentences.usage: Anything you do at a particular time of day — the spine of a routine.
sentences.mnemonic: Four times of day, four single words, no prepositions anywhere.

sentences.cue: In the evening I read a book

words.note: "In the evening", one word, the same frozen shape as утром. Russian's evening runs from about five until it is properly dark, and ночью takes over after that — the split is earlier than the English one.

sentences.trap: книгу still carries M3's object ending. A time word at the front changes nothing about what happens at the back of the sentence.
sentences.sound: VYE-che-ram ya chee-TA-yoo KNEE-goo. Three of the four vowels in вечером are unstressed and flatten right down; only the first is fully said.

variations.cue: In the evening I read a newspaper
variations.changed: swap the thing read — and it bends the same way, being feminine too

variations.cue: In the evening I don't read
variations.changed: не in front of the verb, and the object dropped altogether

variations.cue: Do you read in the evening?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, with the time word at the end

mistake.why: книга is the subject shape. As the thing being read it is книгу — M3's ending, still doing its job.

sentences.usage: Evening routines — and the frame takes any of M3's verbs.
sentences.mnemonic: The front of the sentence and the back of it mind their own business.

words.note: "Every day", learned as one phrase. каждый is "every" and день is "day" — masculine, which is why каждый ends the way it does. The phrase normally sits at the end of the sentence.

sentences.trap: Russian's one present tense is doing double duty here. Я работаю каждый день is a habit, and Я работаю on its own could be either "I work" or "I am working right now" — the time word is what settles it.
sentences.sound: ya ra-BO-ta-yoo KAZH-dy dyen'. The ж of каждый is the s in English "measure"; the ь at the end of день softens the н without adding a sound.

variations.changed: swap the verb — the phrase hangs off any of them
не in front of the verb, and the phrase does not move
the polite you-form — pattern I, so the ending is -ете

mistake.why: The phrase is fixed and singular: каждый день, one day at a time, however many of them there are.

sentences.usage: Routines, jobs, habits — and the single most useful time phrase on this rung.
sentences.mnemonic: Every day, one day: Russian counts them one at a time.

words.note: Often. Words like this go in front of the verb in Russian, where English usually puts them after it or at the end. Never changes shape.

sentences.trap: The word order is the delta: Russian says "I often read" and English says "I read often". Both orders exist in English; only one is ordinary in Russian.
sentences.sound: ya CHA-sta chee-TA-yoo. The т of часто is barely said between the с and the о — a cluster Russian smooths over.

variations.changed: swap the verb — часто keeps its place in front of it
не in front of часто, because it is часто that is being denied
the polite you-form, as a question

mistake.why: Understandable, and it puts the emphasis on "often" rather than saying it plainly. The neutral order is Я часто читаю.

sentences.usage: Saying how much you do something — часто, всегда and иногда all sit in the same slot.
sentences.mnemonic: How often comes before what you do.

words.note: Always, and it takes the same slot as часто, in front of the verb. Note the spelling: it is written всегда and said "fsyeg-DA" — the в is an f here, as it is in встаю.

sentences.trap: It looks like it should start with a v sound and it does not. Russian's в takes the voicing of whatever follows, and с is voiceless.
sentences.sound: ya fsyeg-DA pyoo KO-fye. The stress lands right at the end of всегда, which is unusual enough to be worth remembering.

variations.changed: swap the verb — всегда keeps its place in front of it

variations.cue: In the morning I always drink coffee
variations.changed: a time word in front, and всегда still hugs the verb
the polite you-form, with the ё in the ending

mistake.why: That order puts a strange emphasis on "always" and sounds foreign. It belongs in front of the verb: Я всегда пью кофе.

sentences.usage: Habits you never break — and the ordinary way to answer "do you always …?".
sentences.mnemonic: всегда, часто, иногда: all three live in the same seat, in front of the verb.

words.note: "You speak", from говорить — and this is the OTHER ending pattern: -ите for the polite you and -ит for he or she, where работать took -ете and -ет. The pattern is a fact about the verb and has to be learned with it; nothing in the meaning predicts it.

"In Russian", said of the way you speak — a different word from M1's русский язык, which is the language as a thing. Say a language this way after говорить and never the other way: this shape is only for how something is spoken or written.

sentences.trap: M1's русский язык cannot be used here. Вы говорите русский язык is the word-for-word English and it is wrong: speaking a language takes the по-русски shape.
sentences.sound: vy ga-va-REE-tye pa-ROO-skee. Two unstressed о letters in говорите, both flattened to "a", and the pitch rises on по-русски.

variations.changed: говорите → говорю: the answer, in the I-form of pattern II
не in front of the verb — the most useful sentence a beginner owns
the he/she ending of pattern II — говорит, not говорет

mistake.why: That is the English sentence with Russian words in it. Speaking a language takes по-русски: Вы говорите по-русски?

sentences.usage: The most useful question a beginner can ask, and the most useful answer they can give.
sentences.mnemonic: You do not speak a language in Russian — you speak Russian-ly.

words.cue: in the afternoon · during the day
words.note: The frozen shape of день, covering roughly noon to early evening — Russian's day-part does not line up with English "afternoon". Written with ё, always, and said "dnyom".

sentences.trap: It does not mean "in the day" as opposed to "in the night". днём is the middle stretch of the day, sitting between утром and вечером — four parts, not two.
sentences.sound: dnyom ya ra-BO-ta-yoo. One syllable, and it opens with a д and an н together — a cluster English never starts a word with.

variations.changed: swap the verb — the time word keeps its place at the front

variations.cue: In the afternoon I don't work
variations.changed: не in front of the verb; the time word is untouched

variations.cue: Do you work in the afternoon?
variations.changed: the polite you-form, with the time word moved to the end

mistake.why: The same English habit as В утро: there is no preposition in these phrases. It is днём, one word.

sentences.usage: The middle of the day — the piece of a routine English speakers most often get wrong.
sentences.mnemonic: Four words for four parts of the day, and none of them needs a preposition.

words.note: The last of the four, frozen from ночь. Russian's night starts late — around midnight in ordinary use — so somebody arriving at ten in the evening arrives вечером, not ночью.

sentences.trap: сплю is M3's спать with its everyday ending, and it grows a л the way люблю does. The dictionary shape gave no warning of it.
sentences.sound: NO-chyu ya splyoo. Both words end in a soft sound — the ю does the softening in each — and neither is more than one syllable of real weight.

variations.changed: не in front of the verb, and the time word does not move
the polite you-form of pattern II — спите, with the time word at the end
the he/she ending — спит, another pattern II verb

mistake.why: спать is the dictionary shape and only goes after another verb (Я хочу спать). Standing on its own it needs an ending: Ночью я сплю.

sentences.usage: Closing a description of your day — and the last of the four time words.
sentences.mnemonic: The dictionary shape waits behind another verb; on its own, the verb has to say who.

comprehensionPool.cue: In the morning I drink coffee
In the afternoon I read a book
Do you drink coffee in the morning?

comprehensionPool.display: Я всегда встаю в семь часов.
comprehensionPool.cue: I always get up at seven o'clock
